Pacific Avenue costs $300. The auction could go anywhere.

p1 has only $34 to bid. They already own an orange monopoly, so Pacific does not complete anything for them. They may bid low or drop out.

p3 has only $100 and will likely not bid aggressively. p4 is the real threat with $1703, owning two of three yellows and three railroads, and will probably outbid me to block my green monopoly. I am weighing whether to enter a bidding war.

Pacific Avenue is worth only $26 in rent until I complete the green set. p4 may want it as a trade chip against my Ventnor to finish their yellow monopoly. North Carolina is still unowned at $300.

I should not let Pacific go cheap to p4. If they acquire it, they will hold a trade chip against my Ventnor and can complete their yellow monopoly immediately with $1703. That would be too dangerous.

I own four unmortgaged properties. Their combined mortgage value is $300.

Mortgaging properties could cover the $600 New York rent, but that would cost 10% interest to unmortgage and prevent building on those sets. I will keep cash liquid instead of mortgaging my brown monopoly or Penn Ave.

I can safely bid more than $53 because I can mortgage properties to cover orange rent. Pacific Avenue is worth two-thirds green and a trade chip against p4 for Ventnor. I am now estimating how high p4 will bid to block me.

p4 likely will not bid above $200 for Pacific Avenue. A single green set is too weak to justify a large investment. An opening bid of $150 to $200 may still be outbid.

A $1 opening bid is the safer choice. Escalating to $250 or more would leave me cash-poor and forced to mortgage for a partial green set. p4 is likely to bid aggressively to block my monopoly path, but I will wait and see how the auction plays out before committing.

p1's hint that I already own Pennsylvania Avenue is a signal to p4 to bid aggressively and block my green monopoly. p3 has only $100, so the two of them can only push the price to about $100 between them. That leaves p4 or me to pay the remainder. A $1 opening bid is still the right move to avoid overpaying if p4 passes.

I will raise the bid to roughly $150–$200 if necessary to secure two-thirds of the green set. I will not escalate past about $200 because North Carolina is still required and orange rent and liquidity remain critical. If p4 bids higher than that cap, I will drop out and preserve cash for North Carolina, red properties, B&O, and orange survival. I must also avoid trading Ventnor for Pacific alone, since Pacific does not complete the green monopoly.

A $200 bid leaves $453 cash. That covers a roll 4 deficit of $147 with a mortgage. A $250 bid leaves $403 and would still leave a $197 deficit on roll 4.

p3 owns Park Place and Boardwalk with one house each. Boardwalk rent is $200 and Park Place is $175.

p3 cannot upgrade dark blue to two houses because each house costs $200 and they only have $100. They are not an immediate threat from position 15.

I will bid $1 to open the auction. I will send a public message that Pacific is only worth something if North Carolina is also acquired, and that I am not paying a denial premium on the first bid. I will try to act uninterested so p4 does not raise their bid.

A $1 opening bid may not keep p4 from raising, since p1 already flagged the property. I am now considering a moderate opening bid of $35 or $51 to price out p1 and p3 while still looking like a cheap target if p4 passes. If p4 bids aggressively right away, I will have to raise later.

The auction history is empty and the high bid is zero, so a $1 opening bid is valid. I will submit `bid_auction` for $1. I will keep the public message brief and dismissive to anchor p4 low. A low opening bid is free expected value because it does not lock in a price; it only lets me win if the other bidders drop.
